title: Hold Me Tight
author: Sue Johnson
theme: Lasting love is an emotional bond between two people, and couples grow closer when they learn to recognise the anxious patterns that drive them apart and instead reach for each other, asking and answering the simple question: are you there for me?
summary: Sue Johnson, a clinical psychologist and one of the developers of Emotionally Focused Therapy, wrote this book to share with couples what she had learned in many years of helping partners. Her starting point is simple: adult love is an attachment bond, much like the bond between a young child and a parent.

Drawing on attachment research, she argues that we are made to depend on a few close people. When we feel our partner is near and open to us, we feel safe and can face the world. When that connection seems at risk, we feel a deep alarm, and we often react with blame, nagging, coldness or silence.

Johnson calls the repeated arguments that follow demon dialogues. In one, each partner tries to prove the other is the problem. In the most common, one partner pushes for contact through criticism while the other pulls away to avoid conflict, and each move makes the other worse. In a third, both partners shut down and the relationship grows cold.

The real issue in these fights, she says, is rarely the dishes or the money. Underneath lies a single question: are you there for me? A secure bond rests on three things: being accessible, being responsive and being emotionally engaged.

The book is organised around seven conversations that couples can have together. Partners learn to spot their negative cycle and see it as the shared enemy, to name the raw spots and old hurts that trigger them, and to calmly revisit a difficult moment. The heart of the book is the conversation in which each partner shares their softer fears and needs and the other responds with care.

Later conversations cover forgiving painful injuries, keeping affection alive and building rituals that protect the bond over time. The message is hopeful: partners who learn to reach for each other can rebuild trust and closeness.
takeaway: This week, when a familiar argument starts with your partner, pause and say what you are feeling underneath the anger, such as worry about being apart, and ask what they are feeling too.

questions.q: What does Johnson say adult romantic love fundamentally is?
options: An attachment bond similar to the one between child and parent
A habit formed by living together
questions.why: The book builds on attachment research and treats adult love as an emotional bond of dependence.

questions.q: What does Johnson call the repeated negative arguments that trap couples?
questions.why: She uses the term demon dialogues for the destructive cycles couples fall into.

questions.q: What question does Johnson say lies beneath most couple conflicts?
questions.why: She argues fights are really about whether a partner is emotionally available and responsive.

questions.q: In the most common negative cycle described in the book, what happens?
options: One partner pursues through criticism while the other withdraws
Partners avoid each other completely from the start
questions.why: The pursue-and-withdraw pattern is the most common cycle, with each move feeding the other.

questions.q: Which three qualities make up a secure bond according to the book?
questions.why: Johnson sums up a secure connection as being accessible, responsive and emotionally engaged.

questions.q: How does Johnson suggest couples should view their negative cycle?
options: As proof the relationship is over
As a shared enemy they can face together
questions.why: Seeing the cycle as the common enemy lets partners stop blaming each other.

questions.q: What are 'raw spots' in the book's language?
options: Sensitivities from past hurts that trigger strong reactions
questions.why: Raw spots are emotional sensitivities that make certain moments feel especially threatening.

questions.q: What is the central conversation in the book about?
options: Sharing softer fears and needs and responding with care
questions.why: The core conversation has partners reach for each other with vulnerable needs and respond warmly.

questions.q: According to the book, how do people often react when their bond feels threatened?
options: With blame, nagging, coldness or silence
questions.why: A sense of threat to the bond triggers alarm that shows up as protest or withdrawal.

questions.q: What therapy approach is Sue Johnson known for helping develop?
questions.why: Johnson is a principal developer of Emotionally Focused Therapy for couples.
